title: POC scoping: latency & throughput SLOs - Quanta Analytics
summary: Discussion to align on POC success criteria for latency and throughput: clarify TTFT vs TPOT requirements, p95/p99 targets, measurement plan (benchmarks, harness), traffic profile, and timeline for a 3-4 week POC. Agreed next steps: share benchmark scripts, customer to provide sample traffic and corpus, Redwood to propose test infra and pricing for dedicated pool.
transcript:
Header: 2027-04-01 15:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Ravi (Redwood SE), Elena (Quanta Head of ML), Tom (Infra), Priya (Product), Marco (DS)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, I'm Maya, AE on the Redwood team, and with me is Ravi, our solutions engineer.
[00:08] Elena: Hi, thanks. I'm Elena, head of ML at Quanta. we want to scope the POC to make sure latency/throughput will meet SLAs for our customer-facing chat product.
[00:16] Ravi: Great. high level, we usually split latency SLOs into TTFT, time to first token, which matters for interactive feels, and TPOT — time per output token or per-token latency — which affects streaming throughput. sometimes folks call it T-P-O-T or token-lat.
[00:28] Tom: mm-hm. we care most about first-character latency because our UX bounces if that is slow, but throughput matters when many users are active.
[00:35] Priya: to add, our product expectation: perceived response must feel instant under normal load. we have target concurrency numbers to share.
[00:41] Ravi: perfect. can you give rough numbers: median concurrent active users, peak concurrent, and average response length?
[00:47] Elena: typical median concurrent sessions: 1,200 active users, peak about 5k. average generated tokens per response is ~60 tokens, 90th percentile about 180.
[00:57] Marco: also relevant: 60% of requests are short prompts (single-turn QA), 40% are multi-turn chat with context.
[01:05] Maya: OK, that's helpful. for POC we usually run two benchmark profiles: interactive profile (emulate chat with caching / prefix KV behavior) and throughput profile (sustained concurrent requests to see tail latencies and per-token time).
[01:16] Elena: what SLOs should we target? our internal bar is p95 perceived latency under 300ms ideally, p99 under 600ms.
[01:25] Ravi: we can translate that into TTFT and TPOT targets. from experience, for a 60-token response, the big user-perceived number is TTFT p95 <= 200-300ms. TPOT p95 is typically measured in ms per token — we aim for p95 ~ 15-30ms/token for inference on modern GPU-backed runtimes. p99 will be higher, maybe 40-60ms/token depending on model/quantization.
[01:44] Tom: are those numbers for hosted or dedicated? we assume dedicated GPU pools will be faster but costlier.
[01:49] Ravi: yes dedicated tends to give more predictable p99 tail because you avoid noisy neighbors. hosted can often meet medians but tails are less predictable without reserved capacity. for the POC we should test both if possible — run on Redwood Dedicated config and on our hosted fleet fallback.
[02:01] Priya: what about TTFT vs TPOT tradeoff? we care most about TTFT for UX, but if TPOT is very high it increases cost and can increase TTFT for long responses.
[02:11] Ravi: exactly. TTFT covers model load, KV cache hit/miss, compilation/warmup and first-token compute. TPOT covers the steady-state per-token generation. our measurement plan will isolate cold vs warm (KV prefix cache warm) and measure with and without quantization.
[02:25] Elena: can you propose concrete acceptance criteria for the POC?
[02:29] Maya: sure. proposal: interactive scenario (concurrency simulating 1,200 median, 5k peak burst): TTFT p95 <= 250ms, TTFT p99 <= 450ms. throughput scenario (sustained burst to emulate 5k concurrent): average TPOT p95 <= 25ms/token, TPOT p99 <= 50ms/token, and 99th tail of request-level latency for full response under 800ms for 60-token median.
[02:53] Marco: 800ms p99 for a 60-token response? that would be great if achievable.
[02:57] Ravi: note that for longer responses (180 tokens) the per-token cost accumulates; we'll use per-token SLOs for scaling decisions. also will surface cost numbers so you can evaluate dedicated pool pricing.
[03:08] Tom: measurement specifics — what harness do you need?
[03:12] Ravi: we'll provide a benchmark harness (python load-generator + GH repo link) that can replay real-like traffic. ideally you give us: sample prompt corpus, session-level turn distribution (how many turns per session), and desired concurrency profiles. we'll run experiments then share raw histograms (p50/p95/p99) and token-level timing traces.
[03:29] Priya: sample corpus — we can scrub PII and share a synthetic set. how long will the tests run?
[03:34] Maya: recommended is multi-phase: 1) quick smoke (1 day) to sanity check config; 2) steady-state benchmarks (3-5 days) to collect tail statistics; 3) stress tests (1-2 days) to validate scaling/fallbacks. overall POC timeline ~3-4 weeks including tuning and review.
[03:52] Elena: do you simulate KV cache behavior? our multi-turn chat heavily benefits from prefix caching.
[03:56] Ravi: yes, harness has options to replay prefixes to simulate warm KV cache and to randomize to simulate cold starts. we'll run both. also will measure effective throughput with and without prefix cache. sometimes the transcription in our notes reads K-V cash, sorry, that's K-V cache.
[04:10] Tom: what telemetry will you provide? we'll need per-request traces, per-token timing, CPU/GPU utilization, and logs for failed requests.
[04:17] Maya: we'll provide per-request latency histograms, flamegraphs for kernels if we run on Redwood Dedicated, GPU utilization metrics, and a CSV export of raw samples. we'll also include config (model variant, quantization, batch size).
[04:28] Elena: security notes — we need to run this in our VPC for the POC or at least in a customer-dedicated environment because of data handling. is that possible?
[04:34] Ravi: for POC we can offer a Redwood Dedicated trial in a customer VPC or a Private deployment depending on timeline. quick path is dedicated pool in a customer VPC with our control plane talking via secure tunnels. we'll share SOC2 and network architecture docs.
[04:46] Priya: timeline for setting up dedicated in our VPC?
[04:49] Ravi: typically 3-7 business days for a trial dedicated pool with standard onboarding, could be longer if you need HSM or strict firewall rules. for the POC we can start with hosted benchmarking to iterate quickly, then switch to dedicated for tail testing.
[05:02] Elena: ok. what benchmarks specifically will prove success?
[05:06] Maya: success criteria for POC: 1) meet agreed TTFT p95/p99 targets under your expected concurrency; 2) meet TPOT per-token p95/p99 thresholds for the median response length; 3) demonstrated cost/unit estimates (tokens/sec and dollars per 1M tokens) within your budget targets; 4) no critical security blockers (SSO/SAML, audit logs, KMS integration).
[05:27] Marco: budget targets — we can provide a sense, but want Redwood's estimate to compare.
[05:31] Maya: we'll provide a model-level cost estimate and a recommended quantization profile to hit cost/latency balance.
[05:37] Tom: how do we measure end-to-end from client to first token? does your harness include network latency?
[05:42] Ravi: yes we can run the client-side load generator from your VPC (preferred) or from our region and measure the full round-trip. we'll tag metrics so you can separate network vs inference compute. we'll also run internal-only measurements that exclude client network to isolate compute latency.
[05:58] Priya: any risks / gotchas?
[06:00] Ravi: a few: model cold starts and JIT-like compilation can add a big first-time TTFT; that's why we recommend warming runs and measuring both cold and warm; quantization sometimes increases token latency unpredictably for some models; noisy neighbors on shared hosted fleet can spike p99s.
[06:14] Elena: ok agreed. can you write up the measurement plan and acceptance criteria in a short doc?
[06:18] Maya: yes, we'll send a benchmark plan that includes: scenario definitions, request distributions, metrics to collect (TTFT p50/p95/p99, TPOT p50/p95/p99, total response latency p95/p99), and pass/fail thresholds.
[06:29] Marco: also include how you'll measure per-token (TPOT) — is that measured in the runtime or inferred from deltas between token events?
[06:35] Ravi: we'll instrument at the runtime to capture token emission timestamps (server side) and also record client-observed deltas to reconcile. some transcriptions sometimes call that token-delta, but it's precise in our harness.
[06:45] Priya: for acceptance, what if we meet p95 but not p99? do you have mitigation strategies?
[06:50] Maya: mitigation options: pin to dedicated pool, enable autoscaling with headroom, use smaller model variants as fallback, or degrade gracefully (send shorter responses) under extreme load. we'll propose an A/B rollout plan and automatic fallback rules as part of the POC runbook.
[07:06] Elena: sounds good. next steps?
[07:09] Maya: recap of next steps: 1) Redwood: share benchmark harness repo, measurement doc, and pricing for dedicated pool; 2) Quanta: share scrubbed prompt corpus and session distribution, confirm whether POC should run in your VPC; 3) schedule kickoff for hosted smoke test next week.
[07:24] Tom: I'll start getting the corpus scrubbed and send network contacts.
[07:27] Marco: I'll give sample turn distributions and 95/99 response length stats.
[07:31] Priya: schedule the kickoff — mornings PST work best.
[07:34] Maya: great. we'll aim to deliver the harness and plan by Tuesday. thanks everyone.
[07:39] Elena: thanks, bye.

Auto-summary (from call): agreed POC acceptance criteria centered on TTFT p95 <= 250ms, p99 <= 450ms for interactive; TPOT p95 <= 25ms/token, p99 <= 50ms/token for throughput; measurement plan to include warm/cold runs, per-token instrumentation, and both hosted + dedicated runs. POC timeline ~3-4 weeks.

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-heard acronyms (K-V cash for K-V cache, T-P-O-T spelled out as T-P-O-T), some speaker overlaps near the end.
